units.title: Hello, Bash
units.summary: Write your first Bash script, print text with echo and printf, and learn how to run a script.

lesson.md: **Bash** is a shell: a program that reads commands and runs them. You can type commands in a terminal, one at a time, or save them in a text file. Such a file is a **script**. Bash runs its commands from top to bottom. The command `echo` prints its arguments, followed by a new line.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Hello, Bash"

lesson.md: The first line, `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, is the **shebang**. `#!` tells the system which program runs the file, and `/usr/bin/env bash` finds the `bash` program on your computer. Write it as the very first line of every script.

Save the script in a file, for example `hello.sh`. In the terminal, run it with `bash hello.sh`. You can also make the file executable once with `chmod +x hello.sh` and then start it with `./hello.sh`. The `./` means: the file in the current folder.
The next examples leave out the shebang line to keep them short. Put it at the top of your own scripts.

Bash splits a command into words at spaces. `echo` prints its words with one space between them, so extra spaces disappear. Quotes keep text together exactly as written: double quotes `"..."` or single quotes `'...'`.

lesson.code:
echo Hello     Bash
echo "Hello     Bash"
echo 'one   two'
lesson.output:
Hello Bash
Hello     Bash
one   two

lesson.md: `echo -n` prints without the new line at the end, so the next output continues on the same line. `echo` without arguments prints an empty line. `;` separates two commands on one line. `#` starts a **comment**: Bash ignores the rest of the line.

lesson.code:
echo -n "Hello, "; echo "Bash"
echo
# echo "Hidden"
echo "Done"

lesson.md: `printf` prints text in a format. It does not add a new line, so you write `\n` where a line should end. In the format, `%s` is a placeholder for a string and `%d` for a whole number. The values follow the format. With more values than placeholders, `printf` repeats the format.

lesson.code:
printf "Hello
"
printf "%s is %d years old
" "Ada" 36
printf "%s
" apple banana
lesson.output:
Hello
Ada is 36 years old
apple
banana

card: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is the first line of a script (shebang)
`echo "text"` prints a line, `echo -n` prints without a new line
`#` starts a comment, `;` separates two commands

units.title: Variables
units.summary: Store values in variables, use quotes correctly, catch the output of commands and calculate with whole numbers.

lesson.md: A **variable** stores a value under a name. Write `name=value` to create it. There must be **no spaces** around `=`. To use the value, write `$` before the name: `$name`.

lesson.code:
name="Ada"
age=36
echo "$name is $age years old"

lesson.md: `name = "Ada"` with spaces is an error. Bash then thinks that `name` is a command with the arguments `=` and `Ada`. You get the error `name: command not found`.
`${name}` is the same as `$name`. The braces show where the name ends. You need them when letters or digits follow the name directly. A variable that does not exist is empty.

lesson.code:
fruit="apple"
echo "${fruit}s"
echo "[$fruits]"

lesson.md: Inside double quotes, Bash replaces `$name` with its value. Inside single quotes, nothing is replaced: the text stays exactly as written. Put variables in double quotes when you use them, like `"$text"`. Without quotes, Bash splits the value into words, and extra spaces disappear.

lesson.code:
city="Paris"
text="a    b"
echo "I live in $city"
echo 'I live in $city'
echo $text
echo "$text"
lesson.output:
I live in Paris
I live in $city
a b
a    b

lesson.md: `$(command)` runs a command and puts its output in that place. This is called **command substitution**. You can store the output in a variable. `${#name}` gives the number of characters in a value.

lesson.code:
word=$(echo "hello")
echo "The word is $word"
echo "It has ${#word} characters"
lesson.output:
The word is hello
It has 5 characters

lesson.md: Bash stores values as text. To calculate, write the expression inside `$(( ))`. Inside, you can leave out the `$` before variable names. You can use `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%` (the remainder of a division). Bash calculates with whole numbers only: `/` drops the decimal part. Without the `$`, `(( ))` changes a variable: `(( count += 5 ))` adds `5` to `count`.

card: `"$name"` or `"${name}"` uses the value, `${#name}` is its length
`"..."` replaces variables, `'...'` keeps the text as written
`word=$(echo "hi")` stores the output of a command

units.title: Script arguments
units.summary: Read the arguments of a script with $1, $2, $# and "$@", move them with shift and set default values.

lesson.md: You can give a script values when you start it: `bash greet.sh Ada 36`. These values are the **arguments** of the script. Inside the script, `$1` is the first argument, `$2` the second, and so on. `$0` is the name of the script.

The examples on this page cannot use a command line, so they set the arguments with `set --`. The line `set -- Ada 36` works as if you started the script with the arguments `Ada` and `36`. In a real script, leave out this line.

lesson.code:
set -- Ada 36
echo "Name: $1"
echo "Age: $2"

lesson.md: `$#` is the number of arguments. An argument that was not given is empty. From the tenth argument on, you need braces: `${10}`.

lesson.code:
set -- red green blue
echo "$# arguments"
echo "Third: $3"
echo "Fourth: [$4]"

lesson.md: `"$@"` stands for all arguments, each one as a separate word. Always write it with double quotes: then an argument with a space stays one argument. `"$*"` joins all arguments into one text, with spaces between them.

lesson.code:
set -- "New York" Paris
printf "[%s]\n" "$@"
printf "[%s]\n" $@
echo "All: $*"

lesson.md: `shift` removes the first argument. The others move down: `$2` becomes `$1`, `$3` becomes `$2`, and `$#` gets one smaller. This is useful when the first argument is special, for example a command name.

lesson.code:
set -- copy a.txt b.txt
action=$1
shift
echo "Action: $action"
echo "Files: $*"
echo "Count: $#"
lesson.output:
Action: copy
Files: a.txt b.txt
Count: 2

lesson.md: `${1:-guest}` gives the value of `$1`, or the text `guest` when `$1` is empty or missing. This works with every variable, for example `${name:-nobody}`. `set --` without values removes all arguments.

card: `$1`, `$2` … are the arguments, `$0` is the script name
`"$@"` gives all arguments, each one separate

exercises.explain: `$#` is the number of arguments: `a`, `b`, `c` and `d`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Make decisions with if, test numbers and text in [[ ]], combine commands with && and ||, and choose with case.

lesson.md: `if` runs commands only when a condition is true. The test goes inside `[[ ]]`, with a space after `[[` and before `]]`. The `;` ends the test, `then` starts the commands, `else` starts the commands for a false test, and `fi` (`if` written backwards) ends the block.

lesson.code:
age=16
if [[ $age -ge 18 ]]; then
    echo "adult"
else
    echo "child"
fi

lesson.md: For numbers, use `-eq` (equal), `-ne` (not equal), `-lt` (less than), `-le` (less or equal), `-gt` (greater than) and `-ge` (greater or equal). `elif` (else if) checks another condition when the first one is false. You can also compare numbers inside `(( ))` with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`.

lesson.code:
temp=15
if [[ $temp -gt 25 ]]; then
    echo "hot"
elif [[ $temp -gt 10 ]]; then
    echo "mild"
else
    echo "cold"
fi
if (( temp * 2 >= 30 )); then
    echo "double is at least 30"
fi

lesson.md: For text, use `==` (equal) and `!=` (not equal). `-z` is true when a value is empty, and `-n` when it is not empty. On the right side of `==`, `*` is a pattern that matches any text: `[[ $file == *.jpg ]]` is true for every name that ends in `.jpg`.

lesson.code:
name="Ada"
file="photo.jpg"
if [[ $name == "Ada" ]]; then
    echo "Hi, Ada"
fi
if [[ -z $nickname ]]; then
    echo "no nickname"
fi
if [[ $file == *.jpg ]]; then
    echo "image"
fi

lesson.md: `<` and `>` inside `[[ ]]` compare text in alphabetical order, not numbers. So `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` is true, because `1` comes before `9`. For numbers, use `-lt`, `-gt` or `(( ))`.

Every command ends with an **exit status**: `0` means success, any other number means failure. A test in `[[ ]]` has the status `0` when it is true. `a && b` runs `b` only when `a` succeeds. `a || b` runs `b` only when `a` fails. Inside `[[ ]]`, `&&` means and, `||` means or, and `!` turns true into false.

lesson.code:
x=7
[[ $x -gt 5 ]] && echo "greater than 5"
[[ $x -gt 10 ]] || echo "not greater than 10"
if [[ $x -gt 0 && $x -lt 10 ]]; then
    echo "one digit"
fi
if [[ ! $x -eq 3 ]]; then
    echo "not 3"
fi
lesson.output:
greater than 5
not greater than 10
one digit
not 3

lesson.md: `case` compares one value with several patterns. Each pattern ends with `)`, and each branch ends with `;;`. `|` separates patterns that share a branch, and `*` matches everything else. `esac` (`case` written backwards) ends the block.

card: `a && b` runs `b` on success, `a || b` on failure

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat commands with for over lists and ranges, C-style for and while, and control loops with break and continue.

lesson.md: `for` repeats commands for every word in a list. In each round, the variable gets the next word. The commands go between `do` and `done`.

lesson.code:
for fruit in apple banana cherry; do
    echo "I like $fruit"
done
lesson.output:
I like apple
I like banana
I like cherry

lesson.md: `{1..5}` creates the numbers from `1` to `5`. This is called **brace expansion**. A third number sets the step: `{1..10..3}` counts in steps of `3`. Letters work too: `{a..e}`.

lesson.output:
Round 1
Round 2
Round 3
1 4 7 10
a b c d e

lesson.md: Brace expansion does not work with variables: with `n=3`, `{1..$n}` stays the text `{1..3}`. Use a C-style loop for that.
`for (( i = 1; i <= n; i++ ))` has three parts: the start value, the condition, and the step. The loop runs while the condition is true. `i++` adds `1` to `i`.

lesson.code:
n=4
for (( i = 1; i <= n; i++ )); do
    echo "$i squared is $(( i * i ))"
done
lesson.output:
1 squared is 1
2 squared is 4
3 squared is 9
4 squared is 16

lesson.md: `while` repeats commands as long as a test is true. Make sure that something in the loop changes the test, or the loop never ends. `until` is the opposite: it repeats until the test becomes true.

lesson.code:
count=3
while [[ $count -gt 0 ]]; do
    echo "$count"
    count=$((count - 1))
done
echo "Go"

lesson.md: `break` leaves the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and starts the next one.

lesson.code:
for i in {1..10}; do
    if (( i % 2 == 0 )); then
        continue
    fi
    if (( i > 7 )); then
        break
    fi
    echo "$i"
done

card: `for x in a b c; do … done`
`for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do … done`
`break` leaves the loop, `continue` starts the next round

exercises.prompt: What does this print?

exercises.explain: The loop adds `2`, `4` and `6` to `total`, which gives `12`.

exercises.explain: `{1..10..3}` gives `1 4 7 10`, so the loop runs four times.

exercises.explain: When `i` is `3`, `break` leaves the loop before `echo` runs. `1245` would be the result of `continue`.

exercises.explain: Brace expansion happens before Bash replaces variables, so `{1..$n}` is not a range. The loop runs once with the text `{1..3}`.

exercises.explain: The loop must stop before `3`, so the condition is `i < 3`. `-lt` does not work inside `(( ))`.

`continue` skips only the rest of the current round. `break` ends the whole loop.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Group commands in functions, pass arguments, use local variables, return results and check exit codes with $?.

lesson.md: A **function** is a group of commands with a name. You define it once with `name() { … }`, and then you call it by its name, like a command. Define a function before you call it.

lesson.output:
Hello
Welcome to Bash
Hello
Welcome to Bash

lesson.md: Functions get arguments like scripts do. Inside a function, `$1`, `$2`, `$#` and `"$@"` are the arguments of the function call.

lesson.output:
Hello, Ada. You are 36.
Hello, Bob. You are 25.

lesson.md: Variables in Bash are **global**: a function can read and change the variables of the whole script. `local` creates a variable that exists only inside the function. Use `local` for the variables of a function, unless you want to change a global variable.

lesson.code:
name="Ada"
change() {
    local name="Bob"
    echo "Inside: $name"
}
change
echo "Outside: $name"

lesson.md: To give a value back, the function prints it with `echo`. The caller catches the output with `$( )`, like the output of any other command.

`return` ends a function and sets its exit status. `0` means success, or yes. `$?` holds the exit status of the last command. Because `if` checks an exit status, you can use a function as the test of an `if`.

lesson.code:
is_even() {
    if (( $1 % 2 == 0 )); then
        return 0
    fi
    return 1
}
is_even 4
echo "$?"
is_even 7
echo "$?"
if is_even 10; then
    echo "10 is even"
fi

lesson.md: `return` is not for results: it only gives an exit status from `0` to `255`. Use `echo` for real values. `$?` changes after every command, so read it right after the command you want to check.

card: `$1`, `$#` and `"$@"` are the arguments of the function
`local x=5` exists only inside the function
`return 1` sets the exit status, `$?` reads it

units.title: Pipes and text
units.summary: Write files with > and >>, connect commands with pipes, and work with text using grep, sort, uniq, wc, cut and tr.

lesson.md: `>` sends the output of a command into a file instead of the screen. It creates the file, or overwrites it when it exists. `>>` adds the output to the end of a file. `cat` prints the content of a file.

lesson.code:
echo "apple" > fruits.txt
echo "banana" >> fruits.txt
echo "cherry" >> fruits.txt
cat fruits.txt
echo "kiwi" > fruits.txt
cat fruits.txt

lesson.md: A **here-doc** gives a command several lines of input. `<<EOF` starts it, and a line with only `EOF` ends it. Bash replaces variables inside. With `cat > note.txt <<EOF`, the lines go into a file.

lesson.code:
name="Ada"
cat > note.txt <<EOF
Hello, $name
This is line two.
EOF
cat note.txt
lesson.output:
Hello, Ada
This is line two.

lesson.md: The **pipe** `|` sends the output of one command to the next command as its input. `sort` sorts lines, `sort -r` sorts in reverse, and `sort -n` sorts numbers by their value. `uniq` removes a line when it repeats the line before it, so you usually sort first. `head -n 2` keeps the first two lines. `<` reads the input of a command from a file.

lesson.code:
printf "%s\n" cherry apple banana apple > fruits.txt
sort fruits.txt
echo "---"
sort fruits.txt | uniq
echo "---"
sort -r < fruits.txt | head -n 2
lesson.output:
apple
apple
banana
cherry
---
apple
banana
cherry
---
cherry
banana

lesson.md: `grep word file` prints the lines that contain `word`. `-i` ignores the difference between capital and small letters, `-v` prints the lines that do not contain the word, and `-c` counts the matching lines.

lesson.code:
cat > log.txt <<EOF
INFO start
ERROR disk full
INFO working
error network down
EOF
grep "ERROR" log.txt
echo "---"
grep -i -c "error" log.txt
grep -v "INFO" log.txt
lesson.output:
ERROR disk full
---
2
ERROR disk full
error network down

lesson.md: `cut -d, -f1` splits each line at the character `,` and keeps field `1`. `tr a-z A-Z` replaces characters, here small letters with capital letters, and `tr -d " "` deletes all spaces. `wc -l` counts lines.

lesson.code:
cat > people.csv <<EOF
Ada,36,London
Bob,25,Paris
Eve,41,Rome
EOF
cut -d, -f1 people.csv | tr a-z A-Z
cut -d, -f2,3 people.csv | sort -n
wc -l < people.csv | tr -d " "

lesson.md: On some systems, `wc -l` prints spaces before the number. `tr -d " "` removes them, so your script prints the same everywhere.

card: `cmd > file` writes, `cmd >> file` appends, `cmd < file` reads
`cmd1 | cmd2` sends the output to the next command

exercises.explain: After `sort`, the two `a` lines are next to each other, and `uniq` keeps one of them: `a`, `b` and `c` are 3 lines.

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Store lists in indexed arrays, loop over them, count their elements and use declare -A for arrays with text keys.

lesson.md: An **array** stores several values in one variable. Create it with parentheses: `fruits=(apple banana cherry)`. Each value is an **element** with a number, its **index**. The index starts at `0`. To read an element, write `${fruits[0]}`, with braces.

lesson.code:
fruits=(apple banana cherry)
echo "${fruits[0]}"
echo "${fruits[2]}"
fruits[1]="mango"
echo "${fruits[1]}"

lesson.md: `"${fruits[@]}"` gives all elements, each one as a separate word. `${#fruits[@]}` is the number of elements. `+=( )` adds elements at the end.

lesson.code:
fruits=(apple banana)
fruits+=(cherry)
echo "${fruits[@]}"
echo "${#fruits[@]} fruits"

lesson.md: `$fruits` without an index gives only the first element. And without braces, `$fruits[1]` is the first element followed by the text `[1]`, so it prints `apple[1]`. Always write `${fruits[1]}`.
To go through all elements, write `for x in "${arr[@]}"`. Keep the double quotes: then an element with a space stays one element.

lesson.code:
cities=("New York" "Paris" "Tokyo")
for city in "${cities[@]}"; do
    echo "City: $city"
done
lesson.output:
City: New York
City: Paris
City: Tokyo

lesson.md: `"${!arr[@]}"`, with `!`, gives the indexes instead of the elements. Use it when you need the index and the element.

lesson.code:
colors=(red green blue)
for i in "${!colors[@]}"; do
    echo "$i: ${colors[$i]}"
done

lesson.md: `declare -A` creates an **associative array**. Its keys are text instead of numbers, so you can store a value for every name. `${#ages[@]}` and `"${!ages[@]}"` work here too. This needs Bash 4 or newer.

lesson.code:
declare -A ages
ages[Ada]=36
ages[Bob]=25
echo "Ada is ${ages[Ada]}"
ages[Bob]=26
echo "Bob is ${ages[Bob]}"
echo "${#ages[@]} people"

lesson.md: The keys of an associative array come in no fixed order. When the order matters, sort them: `printf "%s\n" "${!ages[@]}" | sort`.

card: `arr=(a b c)`, `${arr[0]}` is the first element, `arr+=(d)` appends
`"${arr[@]}"` all elements, `${#arr[@]}` their number, `"${!arr[@]}"` the indexes
